idiom_name: member function defined in-class and composed of private member-function calls
implementation_notes: A member function defined inside the class definition is implicitly inline, so the coordinator costs nothing extra once inlined and its steps stay ordinary member functions; declaring them private keeps them out of the class's interface, and protected turns a step into a deliberate hook for subclasses. The classic separate definition (declaration in the class, body in a .cpp file) is still the right choice when the header must stay light or the body would pull heavy includes into every translation unit.
pitfalls: A coordinator defined out of class in a .cpp file, with its steps defined in-class, splits the readable skeleton from the step bodies; keep one style per hierarchy.
Every non-private, non-final member function is virtual-capable: making a step virtual for subclass overrides adds an indirection per call and blocks inlining in hot paths.
In-class definitions are implicitly inline, so a step with a large body is instantiated into every translation unit that includes the header (code bloat, longer builds).
